analysis.one_liner: Bars senior political officials from owning or trading stocks and betting on prediction markets.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on September 16, 2026 and referred to four House committees, with no cosponsors and no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal law to stop certain senior political officials from owning or trading individual stocks, and from betting on prediction markets, while they hold office. The aim is to prevent officials from using their positions, or inside knowledge of upcoming government decisions, to make money in financial markets. As of now the bill has only been introduced and sent to committees, with no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens benefit from a rule that reduces the chance that officials who shape laws, regulations, and contracts can personally profit from stock trades or prediction-market bets tied to those decisions. Ethical-government advocates and the members' own constituents also gain a clearer separation between officials' public duties and private investments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens watching for conflicts of interest

how_it_helps.text: It would prohibit covered political officials from owning or trading individual stocks, removing the chance that they can personally profit from laws, contracts, or regulatory decisions they influence.
It would also bar these officials from trading on prediction markets, closing a related avenue to bet on events their own actions could affect.

analysis.who_pays: Covered political officials would bear the cost: they could no longer hold individual stocks or trade prediction markets, and would have to move their investments into vehicles like blind trusts or broad index funds. The brokerage industry would lose a small number of accounts and trading activity.

drawbacks.text: The bill places a blanket restriction on owning or trading individual stocks for covered officials, which critics of such bans argue deters qualified people from seeking office or requires their assets to be shifted into blind trusts or diversified funds, at some personal cost and complexity.
With zero cosponsors and four separate committees holding jurisdiction, the bill faces a long procedural road and, as written, may never reach a floor vote in this Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is a straightforward rule that makes it harder for the officials who write laws to profit from those laws; the costs are compliance burdens and a possible reduction in the pool of candidates willing to serve under strict asset rules, objections that supporters would typically address with blind trusts and qualified holdings. Because the bill has not advanced, neither the benefit nor the costs have been tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to four House committees, and no committee has taken it up, so it has never come up for a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on September 16, 2026.
Its only action since introduction was a referral to four House committees on the same day.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet, so no one has gained or lost from the bill itself; a bill to restrict officials' own investing sits in committee, and the officials it would cover remain free to trade while it does.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; nothing has happened

for.name: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to four House committees.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors of either party and no votes yet, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill would bar certain political officials from holding individual stocks or trading prediction markets, giving up a source of personal investment gain. The direct beneficiaries are ordinary citizens, who get clearer assurance that officials' decisions are not tied to their portfolios.
A trading ban for officials would remove a small set of active trading accounts and reduce demand for personal brokerage services among covered officials. Any effect on the industry overall is small.

analysis.trajectory: Bills like this typically stall when referred to multiple committees, and with zero cosponsors this one has no visible path to a floor vote; unless committee leadership schedules action, it will likely expire when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
